stops.name: Buenos Aires, the GOU and the coup of 1943
stops.campa: On the fourth of June the army marches on the Casa Rosada and sweeps away the corrupt conservative order. Colonel Perón is a founder and hidden engine of the GOU, the Grupo de Oficiales Unidos, the lodge of nationalist officers behind the rising. He takes no throne; he takes the small, despised office of labor. Others reach for war ministries and provinces. Perón, alone among them, sees that power in the twentieth century lies not in the barracks but in the workshops: in the millions of workers no one has ever asked to speak.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Secretaría de Trabajo y Previsión
stops.campa: On the twenty-seventh of November the old Department of Labor is raised into a Secretaría de Trabajo y Previsión, and Perón takes command. From this desk he changes everything: the eight-hour day, paid holidays, the aguinaldo, pensions, labor courts, the statute of the peón. The unions, long ignored and repressed, find in this colonel a patron who signs their demands into law. Worker by worker, contract by contract, he wins the whole laboring class to himself. He will call this the true beginning of his movement: the initial day.
stops.quote: El día que creamos la Secretaría de Trabajo y Previsión, para mí es el día inicial de nuestro movimiento.
stops.quote_source: Juan Perón, on the founding of the Secretaría de Trabajo y Previsión

stops.name: San Juan, the earthquake and the festival of the ruins
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of January the earth heaves and San Juan falls to rubble; ten thousand die beneath their houses. Perón, from Trabajo y Previsión, throws the state into the rescue and the relief, and calls the nation to give. He summons artists and public to a great solidarity festival at Luna Park in Buenos Aires. Out of catastrophe he forges a mystique of the caring state. And out of the festival's crowd, on the twenty-second, a young radio actress will step into his life and change the history of the country.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Luna Park: the meeting with Eva Duarte
stops.campa: On the night of the twenty-second, at the San Juan relief festival in Luna Park, the widower colonel is seated beside a slender radio actress of twenty-four, María Eva Duarte, natural daughter of the provinces, who has climbed from nothing by will alone. They speak, and by the small hours of the twenty-third they are not to part again. She becomes his companion, his voice among the poor and the women, his fiercest instrument. Two ambitions of the humble, meeting; from this night the myth of Perón and Evita is born.
stops.quote_source: Words attributed to Eva Duarte at the Luna Park meeting (Peronist tradition)

stops.name: Isla Martín García, the prisoner in the river
stops.campa: His rivals in the army, terrified of the labor colonel's power, force his resignation and on the thirteenth of October seize him and carry him to the island prison of Martín García in the estuary. There he sits, the whole edifice of his rise apparently thrown down in a week. He writes to Eva; he feigns illness, and a sympathetic doctor certifies a pleurisy, the pretext to bring him back to the continent and the Hospital Militar. In the workshops and the tanneries of the industrial belt, meanwhile, a fury is rising that no barracks can imagine.

stops.name: Plaza de Mayo, the balcony and the descamisados, 17 October 1945
stops.campa: From dawn on the seventeenth the workers pour out of the industrial suburbs and across the bridges into the Plaza de Mayo, in shirtsleeves, sleeves rolled, the descamisados, the shirtless ones, cooling their feet in the fountains under the winter-spring sun. They will not leave until Perón is free. All day the multitude swells and roars his name. At last, near eleven at night, he steps onto the balcony of the Casa Rosada, and a nation of the humble roars back. The people have taken him from prison and set him on the balcony. Peronism is born this day.
stops.quote: Hace casi dos años, desde estos mismos balcones, dije que tenía tres honras en mi vida: la de ser soldado, la de ser un patriota y la de ser el primer trabajador argentino.
stops.quote_source: Juan Perón, speech from the balcony of the Casa Rosada, 17 October 1945

stops.name: Junín, the marriage to Eva
stops.campa: Five days after the balcony, on the twenty-second, Perón and Eva marry at the civil registry in Junín, her home town, Domingo Mercante and her brother Juan Duarte as witnesses. The colonel raised back to power by the people takes as wife the woman who will become their saint. The private bond is sealed just as the public triumph crests. Together now, publicly and lawfully, they turn to the campaign that will make him president: she at his side on every whistle-stop, her voice reaching where his cannot.

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the inauguration, first presidency
stops.campa: Having won the February election against the whole array of the oligarchy and the American ambassador, on the fourth of June Perón takes the presidential sash and the baton in the Casa Rosada. The descamisados fill the plaza again, this time in triumph. He proclaims a new Argentina founded on three banners: political sovereignty, economic independence, social justice; and a Third Position between the empires of capital and communism. The labor colonel is now the constitutional president, and the doctrine of Justicialismo becomes the law of a state.

stops.name: Tucumán, the Declaration of Economic Independence and the First Five-Year Plan
stops.campa: On the ninth of July, anniversary of independence, at the historic house of Tucumán where the fathers once broke from Spain, Perón signs a second declaration, this one of economic independence, and unveils the First Five-Year Plan. The state will industrialize the country, build steel and power at San Nicolás and in Jujuy, throw off the tutelage of foreign capital. He binds the new economic sovereignty to the old political one, standing on the very ground of 1816. Argentina, he declares, will belong to Argentines and above all to those who work her.
stops.quote: Soberanía política, independencia económica y justicia social.
stops.quote_source: Juan Perón, the three banners proclaimed with the First Five-Year Plan, Tucumán, 1947

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the female vote and the rise of Evita
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of September the law is proclaimed: the women of Argentina shall vote. Eva stands at the heart of it, and from the balcony she shows the enacted law to the crowd of women below. She has become a power in her own right: patron of the poor through her Foundation, voice of the shirtless, terror of the oligarchy, building a fervor that will make her, in the eyes of millions, a saint. The Peronist movement now stands on two legs: the conductor Perón and the abanderada Evita.
stops.quote: Mujeres de mi Patria, recibo en este instante, de manos del Gobierno de la Nación, la ley que consagra nuestros derechos cívicos.
stops.quote_source: Eva Perón, on the proclamation of women's suffrage, 23 September 1947

stops.name: Retiro, the nationalization of the railways
stops.campa: On the first of March the British-owned railways pass into Argentine hands, and the state takes formal possession at Retiro. A vast crowd of descamisados fills the plaza before the great terminus; banners read Los ferrocarriles son argentinos: the railways are Argentine. The steel arteries that carried Argentine wealth to the ports for foreign profit are national now. It is the highest emblem of economic independence, the Five-Year Plan made iron and rail, and the crowd celebrates it as a second liberation from empire.
stops.quote_source: Peronist proclamation on the nationalization of the railways, 1 March 1948

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Eva's renunciamiento
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of August a vast open-air Cabildo of the people fills Avenida 9 de Julio, demanding that Eva stand as vice-president beside Perón. She is dying of cancer, though few yet know it, and the army will not have her. Wracked and beloved, she begs the multitude for time, then renounces the honor. Her renunciamiento is a passion play performed before the nation; the poor weep in the streets. She has refused the crown and thereby become greater than any office: the martyr of the descamisados.
stops.quote: Yo no renuncio a la lucha ni al trabajo... renuncio a los honores.
stops.quote_source: Eva Perón, the renunciamiento speech, 22 August 1951
